concepts.name: Euclid's Division Lemma
concepts.simple_definition: For a non-negative integer a and a positive integer b, there are unique whole numbers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that a = b×q + r, where 0 ≤ r < b.
concepts.deep_explanation: This is just the formal statement of long division: dividing a by b always gives a definite quotient and a remainder smaller than the divisor. It is the foundation for tests of divisibility, and for finding GCF and LCM.
concepts.real_example: Dividing 2,574 by 8 gives quotient 321 and remainder 6, so 2,574 = 8 × 321 + 6.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes forget the remainder must satisfy 0 ≤ r < b — if your 'remainder' is equal to or larger than the divisor, the division isn't finished.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] For a non-negative integer a and a positive integer b, there are unique whole numbers q (quotient) and r (remainder) such that a = b×q + r, where 0 ≤ r < b. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Prime and composite numbers
concepts.simple_definition: A prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself); a composite number has more than two factors. 1 is neither.
concepts.deep_explanation: Every number greater than 1 is either prime or composite — this dichotomy is what makes prime factorization possible. Checking for primality typically means checking whether any number divides it besides 1 and itself.
concepts.real_example: 53 is prime (only 1 and 53 divide it); 18 is composite because 1,2,3,6,9,18 all divide it.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often think 1 is prime or that 2 (being even) can't be prime — but 2 is in fact the only even prime number.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] A prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself); a composite number has more than two factors. 1 is neither. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Prime factorization
concepts.simple_definition: Writing a composite number as a product of only prime numbers.
concepts.deep_explanation: Every composite number breaks down into a unique set of prime factors (this uniqueness is the 'fundamental theorem of arithmetic'), which is the basis for finding GCF and LCM efficiently.
concepts.common_confusion: Learners sometimes stop factoring too early, leaving a composite factor (e.g. writing 30 = 2 × 15 without continuing to break 15 into 3 × 5).
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] Writing a composite number as a product of only prime numbers. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.common_confusion_amharic: [አማርኛ] Learners sometimes stop factoring too early, leaving a composite factor (e.g. writing 30 = 2 × 15 without continuing to break 15 into 3 × 5).

concepts.name: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) and Least Common Multiple (LCM)
concepts.simple_definition: The GCF is the largest number that divides two or more numbers exactly; the LCM is the smallest number that all of them divide into exactly.
concepts.deep_explanation: GCF can be found using a Venn diagram of factors or by taking common prime factors with the lowest powers; LCM can be found by listing multiples or by taking all prime factors with the highest powers. A useful shortcut: GCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.
concepts.real_example: For 12 and 18: GCF = 6, LCM = 36, and indeed 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes confuse which one should be smaller — GCF is always ≤ both numbers, while LCM is always ≥ both numbers.

concepts.name: Rational numbers and their decimal forms
concepts.simple_definition: A rational number can be written as a/b where a, b are integers and b ≠ 0. Dividing a by b always produces either a terminating or a repeating decimal.
concepts.deep_explanation: Terminating decimals end after a finite number of digits (division reaches a remainder of 0); repeating decimals have a digit or block of digits that repeats forever, shown with a bar notation. Both types are rational.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes think a long decimal expansion means it's irrational — but as long as it eventually repeats a pattern, it is still rational.
concepts.name_amharic: Rational numbers and their decimal forms (በአማርኛ)
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] A rational number can be written as a/b where a, b are integers and b ≠ 0. Dividing a by b always produces either a terminating or a repeating decimal. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።
concepts.deep_explanation_amharic: [አማርኛ ማብራሪያ] Terminating decimals end after a finite number of digits (division reaches a remainder of 0); repeating decimals have a digit or block of digits that repeats forever, shown with a bar notation. concepts.common_confusion_amharic: [አማርኛ] Students sometimes think a long decimal expansion means it's irrational — but as long as it eventually repeats a pattern, it is still rational.

concepts.name: Converting repeating decimals to fractions
concepts.simple_definition: A technique using algebra (multiplying by a power of 10 and subtracting) to turn a repeating decimal into an exact a/b fraction.
concepts.deep_explanation: The trick is to set d equal to the repeating decimal, multiply both sides by a power of 10 that shifts the decimal point past one full repeating block, then subtract the original equation to cancel the infinite repeating part, leaving a simple equation to solve for d.
concepts.real_example: For d = 0.5̄: 10d = 5.5̄, subtracting d = 0.5̄ gives 9d = 5, so d = 5/9.
concepts.common_confusion: Choosing the wrong power of 10 to multiply by (it must match exactly one full repeating block) leads to an equation that doesn't fully cancel the repeating part.

concepts.real_example_amharic: [አማርኛ] For d = 0.5̄: 10d = 5.5̄, subtracting d = 0.5̄ gives 9d = 5, so d = 5/9.

concepts.name: Irrational numbers
concepts.simple_definition: Decimal numbers that neither terminate nor repeat — they cannot be written as a simple fraction a/b.
concepts.deep_explanation: The square root of any natural number that is not a perfect square is irrational (e.g. √2, √3, √5). Famous constants like π are also irrational. Irrational numbers can still be located on the number line, e.g. using compass-and-straightedge constructions based on the Pythagorean theorem.
concepts.real_example: √2 ≈ 1.4142135624... never settles into a repeating or terminating pattern, so it is irrational.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes assume any square root is irrational — but √25 = 5, which is rational, since 25 is a perfect square.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] Decimal numbers that neither terminate nor repeat — they cannot be written as a simple fraction a/b. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Operations on irrational numbers
concepts.simple_definition: Rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing expressions containing radicals, including combining 'like radicals' (same index and radicand).
concepts.deep_explanation: √a × √b = √(ab) and √a / √b = √(a/b) for a, b > 0. Like radicals (e.g. 2√5 and 3√5) combine the way like terms do in algebra; unlike radicals (e.g. √2 and √3) cannot be combined by addition/subtraction, only by multiplication/division rules.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often try to add √a + √b as if it equals √(a+b) — this is not a valid rule; only multiplication and division combine radicals this way, not addition or subtraction.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] Rules for adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing expressions containing radicals, including combining 'like radicals' (same index and radicand). (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።

concepts.name: Real numbers and their properties
concepts.simple_definition: The set ℝ of all rational and irrational numbers together, which satisfies closure, commutative, associative, distributive, identity, and inverse properties for addition and multiplication.
concepts.deep_explanation: Every real number has an additive inverse (its opposite) so that a + (-a) = 0, and every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse (its reciprocal) so that a × (1/a) = 1. These properties are the algebraic 'rules of the game' that justify manipulating real number expressions.
concepts.real_example: The additive inverse of √2 is -√2, and its multiplicative inverse is 1/√2.
concepts.common_confusion: Zero is the only real number without a multiplicative inverse (reciprocal), since division by zero is undefined.
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] The set ℝ of all rational and irrational numbers together, which satisfies closure, commutative, associative, distributive, identity, and inverse properties for addition and multiplication. (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።
concepts.deep_explanation_amharic: [አማርኛ ማብራሪያ] Every real number has an additive inverse (its opposite) so that a + (-a) = 0, and every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse (its reciprocal) so that a × (1/a) = 1. concepts.real_example_amharic: [አማርኛ] The additive inverse of √2 is -√2, and its multiplicative inverse is 1/√2.
concepts.common_confusion_amharic: [አማርኛ] Zero is the only real number without a multiplicative inverse (reciprocal), since division by zero is undefined.

concepts.name: Intervals and absolute value
concepts.simple_definition: An interval is a set of all real numbers between two endpoints, written with brackets [ ] (endpoint included) or parentheses ( ) (endpoint excluded); absolute value |x| measures a number's distance from zero.
concepts.deep_explanation: Intervals give compact notation for ranges of real numbers, including unbounded ranges using ∞ or -∞. Absolute value is always non-negative: |x| = x when x ≥ 0, and |x| = -x when x < 0 (flipping a negative number to its positive counterpart).
concepts.real_example: [3,5] means all real numbers from 3 to 5 including both ends; |-2| = 2, since -2 is 2 units from zero.
concepts.common_confusion: Students often think |x| always just 'removes the minus sign' without understanding that it's really about distance from zero, which matters when x itself is an unknown or expression.

concepts.name: Laws of exponents (including zero, negative, and fractional powers)
concepts.simple_definition: Rules for simplifying expressions with powers, extended beyond whole numbers to zero exponents (a⁰=1), negative exponents (a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ), and fractional exponents (a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a).
concepts.deep_explanation: The five core laws — product, quotient, power-of-a-power, power-of-a-product, and power-of-a-quotient — all extend consistently to negative and fractional exponents, which is what links exponent notation to radical notation.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes think a negative exponent makes the whole value negative — but a⁻ⁿ just means 'take the reciprocal', not 'make it negative' (e.g. 2⁻¹ = 1/2, a positive number).

concepts.name: Rounding, decimal places, and significant figures
concepts.simple_definition: Three related ways to approximate a number: rounding to a place value (like nearest 100), fixing the number of digits after the decimal point (decimal places), or fixing the total number of meaningful digits counted from the first non-zero digit (significant figures).
concepts.deep_explanation: For all three, you look at the digit just after the cutoff point: if it's 5 or more, round the cutoff digit up; if it's less than 5, leave it unchanged.
concepts.real_example: 28.79 rounded to 3 significant figures is 28.8 (since the digit after, 9, rounds the 7 up to 8).
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes count leading zeros (e.g. in 0.0062) as significant figures — leading zeros before the first non-zero digit never count.
concepts.name_amharic: Rounding, decimal places, and significant figures (በአማርኛ)
concepts.simple_definition_amharic: [አማርኛ] Three related ways to approximate a number: rounding to a place value (like nearest 100), fixing the number of digits after the decimal point (decimal places), or fixing the total number of meaningful digits counted from the first non-zero digit (significant figures). (ይህ ትርጓሜ በኢትዮጵያ የ9ኛ ክፍል ሥርዓተ-ትምህርት መሠረት የተዘጋጀ ነው)።
concepts.deep_explanation_amharic: [አማርኛ ማብራሪያ] For all three, you look at the digit just after the cutoff point: if it's 5 or more, round the cutoff digit up; if it's less than 5, leave it unchanged. — ይህ ጽንሰ-ሐሳብ ተማሪዎች በክፍል ውስጥ የተማሩትን በቀላሉ እንዲረዱ ይረዳቸዋል።
concepts.real_example_amharic: [አማርኛ] 28.79 rounded to 3 significant figures is 28.8 (since the digit after, 9, rounds the 7 up to 8).
concepts.common_confusion_amharic: [አማርኛ] Students sometimes count leading zeros (e.g. in 0.0062) as significant figures — leading zeros before the first non-zero digit never count.

concepts.name: Upper and lower bounds
concepts.simple_definition: The maximum (upper bound) and minimum (lower bound) values a rounded/approximated number could actually have been before rounding.
concepts.deep_explanation: Find the place value of the rounding accuracy, divide it by 2, then add/subtract that amount from the stated value. When approximated numbers are combined (added, subtracted, multiplied), the overall bounds are found by combining the individual bounds in the appropriate direction (e.g. lower + lower for the minimum sum).
concepts.real_example: A weight of 872 kg to the nearest kg has bounds 871.5 ≤ weight < 872.5.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes forget that the upper bound is a strict inequality (< not ≤) because a value exactly at the upper bound would round up to the next number instead.

concepts.name: Scientific (standard) notation
concepts.simple_definition: A way to write very large or very small numbers as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer.
concepts.deep_explanation: Moving the decimal point left (for large numbers) gives a positive exponent equal to the number of places moved; moving it right (for small numbers) gives a negative exponent.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes leave more than one non-zero digit before the decimal point (e.g. writing 18.567 × 10⁸ instead of 1.8567 × 10⁹), which is not proper scientific notation.

concepts.name: Rationalizing the denominator
concepts.simple_definition: Rewriting a fraction with an irrational denominator so that the denominator becomes a rational number, by multiplying by an equivalent form of 1.
concepts.deep_explanation: For a single radical like 1/√a, multiply by √a/√a. For a two-term denominator like 1/(√a - √b), multiply by the 'conjugate' (√a + √b)/(√a + √b), since (√a-√b)(√a+√b) = a - b, a rational number.
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes multiply only the denominator by the rationalizing factor and forget to multiply the numerator by the same factor, which changes the value of the fraction.

concepts.name: Using GCF/LCM and division to solve real-world problems
concepts.simple_definition: Applying GCF (for splitting/grouping into equal maximum-size portions) and LCM (for finding when repeating events coincide) to practical situations.
concepts.deep_explanation: GCF answers 'what is the largest equal-sized group/piece I can make from these quantities?' while LCM answers 'when will these repeating cycles line up again?' Euclid's division lemma answers 'how many equal groups, with what remainder, can I make?'
concepts.real_example: To cut three ropes of 78 cm, 117 cm, and 351 cm into equal pieces of the largest possible length with no leftover, find GCF(78, 117, 351).
concepts.common_confusion: Students sometimes use LCM when the problem calls for GCF (or vice versa) — the key clue is whether the question asks for the largest common 'unit' (GCF) or the smallest number that all values divide into (LCM).
